blocks.text: Names in the File and IDs in the Program

The inspection station's format names its groups red, green, and blue. In memory, we assign them IDs 0, 1, and 2. The name is a textual representation; the ID enables lookup at a small position. The table defines the correspondence: we do not assume that the name of a color is a number.

The order of this table is part of the agreed correspondence. Changing it without adapting the in-memory data would change what each ID means. We can look up a name by index only after checking 0..2; to obtain the index from a name, we need a search.

blocks.question: The text "blue" arrives, and we need its ID. Which operation is appropriate?
options: Use the number of letters in the name as the index.
Search for an exact match in the table.
Read the text as if it were a decimal integer.
blocks.explanation: The matching position for blue is 2. Neither its length nor numeric conversion defines the correspondence.

blocks.text: A Failed Search Does Not Invent an ID

The output consists of two lines: 1:2 and 0:2. On false, the parameter keeps its previous value. Therefore, inspecting id alone is not enough: we must use the bool to determine whether the current search succeeded.

blocks.question: Fill in only the operator that rejects ID 3 and higher, along with the negative-ID check, before calling at().
blocks.explanation: The domain includes 0, 1, and 2. The upper bound excludes 3; it is rejected before the table is accessed.

blocks.question: The search compares entire strings without changing letter case. What happens with "Blue"?
options: It is accepted as 2 because comparison ignores uppercase letters.
It is accepted as 0 because it is the first inexact name.
It is rejected, and the destination retains its value.
blocks.explanation: Blue and blue are different strings. Accepting alternative spellings would require defining and applying another policy.

blocks.text: Identity May Depend on the Group

Each group contains records with IDs 0..9 and a Recuento. Record 7 in red and record 7 in blue are different entities: their complete identity is the group plus the record ID. We do not reject an ID simply because it exists in another group. Within a single group, however, each ID may appear at most once.

blocks.question: We receive (red,7), (blue,7), and (red,7), in that order. If each group forbids duplicate IDs, what is the first conflict?
options: The second record, because ID 7 appears again anywhere.
The third record, because ID 7 repeats within red.
None, because all three IDs are within 0..9.
blocks.explanation: A valid numeric range is not sufficient. The first blue–7 association is new; the second red–7 association repeats an identity within its group.

blocks.text: A flat collection of records would also need to retain the group. A Grupo structure containing its own records represents that scope directly. Do not confuse this identity of the data with the scope of a name declared in the code: these are separate decisions.

blocks.question: Predict both output lines. Each bool indicates the result of the current conversion.
blocks.explanation: ID 1 converts to green. ID 3 is outside the domain and does not change the previous text.

blocks.text: As a review exercise, rebuild buscar_grupo and nombre_grupo without copying them from the earlier examples. Preserve these contracts: an exact name or an ID in 0..2; true updates the destination and false preserves it. Test every name and confirm that the conversion name → ID → name recovers the original. Then test gray, an empty string, Red, and IDs -1 and 3 with different initial destinations.

Decide on the expected outputs before running. A destination that retains a permitted ID after false does not make an unknown input valid. Do not call the inverse conversion as though a failed search had succeeded.
Consult the reference on the following page after building your own solution. Use at() only with a validated index; this exercise does not require a new container.
Later Reference and Change of Representation

The reference produces red:1:1:1, green:1:1:1, and blue:1:1:1, one line per name; it ends with 0:8:0:previous. Criteria: consistent conversions in both directions, checked domain, exact matches, and preserved destinations on false. Also complete the boundary tests requested in the lab.

If a new format version accepts more names or synonyms, we must decide whether the inverse conversion writes the name received or a chosen canonical form. Recovering the data and recovering every original character are not the same goal. The next part defines its own format and closing markers.

Representations and reading structures are covered in the primary source (Stroustrup, 2024, sections 9.9.1–9.9.3, pp. 270–275). The model, format, and activities are original; they review tables, searches, contracts, and presence from this learning path.
